title: Bulgur and Herb Salad
subtitle: Tabbouleh-style bulgar with masses of flat-leaf parsley, tomato and lemon
excerpt: Tabbouleh: much more herb than grain, dressed heavily with lemon juice. Fine bulgur soaked rather than cooked, then mixed with flat-leaf parsley, mint, tomato and spring onion. The parsley is the point of the dish, not the grain.
sourceNotes: Tabbouleh is a Levantine salad from Lebanon and Syria, eaten widely across the Arab world. The defining characteristic is that parsley dominates: authentic tabbouleh has a ratio of roughly four to six parts herb to one part grain. British versions often invert this, making a grain salad with a sprinkle of herb. The classic Lebanese tabbouleh, documented extensively in cookbooks by Claudia Roden, Anissa Helou and Yotam Ottolenghi, uses fine bulgur (No. 1 grade), very fine chopping of the herbs, and abundant lemon juice.

recipe.batchNotes: Best on the day. Keeps for 1 day in the fridge; herbs will wilt slightly.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Soak the bulgur and prep the herbs separately; combine up to 2 hours before serving.

content.text: Tabbouleh is a herb salad, not a grain salad. The bulgur is there to give body and absorb the lemon dressing; the parsley is the flavour and the bulk. Use much more parsley than feels natural. The lemon should be assertive. Fine bulgur (grade 1) soaks in water in 20 minutes without cooking, which is how the dish stays fresh-tasting.

items.prepNote: leaves and thin stems, very finely chopped

content.text: Put {{bulgur-wheat}} of fine bulgur in a bowl and cover with cold water by about 2 cm. Leave to soak for 20 to 30 minutes until tender. Drain through a sieve and squeeze out as much water as possible. Spread on a clean tea towel and press to dry.

Put the bulgur in a large bowl. Add {{parsley-flat}} of finely chopped flat-leaf parsley, {{mint}} of finely chopped mint, the diced tomato and the spring onion. Pour over the juice of {{lemon}} lemons and {{olive-oil}} of olive oil. Add {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt and {{black-pepper}} of pepper. Toss thoroughly and taste. Tabbouleh should taste very sharply of lemon and very green with parsley. Adjust the lemon and salt to taste. Leave for 15 minutes before serving.

items.cause: Bulgur not drained and pressed dry enough, or tomatoes not deseeded.
items.fix: Press the soaked bulgur in a clean cloth. Deseed the tomatoes before dicing and let them drain for 5 minutes on kitchen paper.

items.cause: Not enough herb, lemon or salt, and too much grain.
items.fix: Tabbouleh should have much more herb than grain. Check the ratio: at 80 g bulgur to 150 g herb, the parsley and mint together should visually dominate the bowl.

content.text: Tabbouleh is Lebanon's best-known dish outside the Arab world. In the UK it moved from speciality shops to supermarkets by the 2000s, though most supermarket versions get the herb-to-grain ratio wrong. Claudia Roden called it 'herb salad with grain' rather than 'grain salad with herbs'. What you make at home is a different dish from what most people have bought ready-made.
